newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - REGIONALS SAG, THAI OUTLOOK BETTER.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - REGIONALS SAG, THAI OUTLOOK BETTER.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies lost ground on Friday as players continued to favour the dollar in the face of continuing uncertainty over the region's prospects.

Dealers said the market was still keeping a watchful eye on Thailand's economic rescue package, with interest pinned on the amount of aid it would receive from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other countries.
The IMF said on Thursday it would convene a meeting of interested countries and institutions on August 11 in Tokyo to discuss a financing package for Thailand.
No details of the size of the package have been confirmed but it is widely expected to be in the region of $12-$15 billion.

"If the package goes to $15 billion, it'll restore some confidence in Thailand. And the stock market could see some reprieve from its current low levels," said the head of regional currencies at a European bank in Singapore.

The market had a muted reaction to the Bank of Thailand (BOT)'s announcement on Friday it was setting up a federal deposit insurance scheme to protect deposits of still operating banks and finance companies.
BOT deputy governor Siri Garnjarerndee said the guarantees should last for about two years and should help bring down deposit rates, which he said are "too high".
Dealers said the move had been expected after the BOT's shock closure of 42 more finance firms earlier in the week prompted a run on deposits at smaller institutions.
"The market was expecting them to try and lower deposit rates because they can't have a rescue plan with rates continuing to be so high," the Singapore dealer said.
Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah showed a softer bias after Bank Indonesia cut rates on its short-term certificates for periods of one week and above by 50 basis points.
But the central bank, which has been keeping a tight grip on short-term liquidity to curb speculative dollar purchases, maintained high overnight rates.
The rupiah was at 2,591/61 at 0445 GMT against an opening of 2,585.0/93.0.
The Malaysian ringgit remained under pressure after falling sharply overnight on rumours, later denied, that central bank governor Ahmad Mohamed Don had resigned.
"Dollar/ringgit remains very biddish," said a dealer with another European bank in Singapore. "People are not really buying aggressively but the bids are getting higher."

Dealers said Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's remark that he was concerned with the sharp fall in the ringgit had spurred some caution, but the ringgit looked set to retest its recent low of 2.6530 to the dollar.
"There's been a lot of dollar selling by Kuala Lumpur corporates at 2.6510. But if the dollar breaks above there, the ringgit could head much lower to 2.67 and even 2.70," a Singapore dealer said.
"I don't think the Malaysian authorities can do much about it because these are not just speculative flows. There are actual capital outflows as well," he added.
The ringgit was at 2.6465/90 to the dollar at 0445 GMT against 2.6455/85 late on Thursday.
The Singapore dollar slipped back towards its overnight lows on selling by U.S. hedge funds and dealers said it looked set to test the 1.48 to the U.S. dollar level over the next week.
"I wouldn't be surprised if there are a lot of technical stops and fresh positions put on above 1.48," a dealer said.
The Taiwan dollar was hit by heavy dollar demand despite central bank efforts to prop it up minutes before the close of trade on Thursday.
It was at T$28.754/762 at 0445 GMT against a T$28.639 close.
Dealers said the central bank's intervention on Thursday had not dampened buying interest in the U.S. dollar.
The Philippine peso eased slightly but its falls were expected to be cushioned by dollar sales by banks unloading their excess long positions.
It was at 28.50/55 to the dollar against a previous close at 28.46. Manila traders said there was corporate buying interest for the dollar around the 28.45 peso level.
